Supreme People's Court

Notice on Issuing Two Sets of Answers to Questions Concerning the Specific Application of the Economic Contract Law in the Trial of Economic Contract Dispute Cases and the Specific Application of the Civil Procedure Law (for Trial Implementation) in the Trial of Economic Dispute Cases

Fa (Jing) Fa [1987] No. 20

To all local people's courts at various levels, military courts at various levels, railway transport courts, and maritime courts:

The "Answers to Questions Concerning the Specific Application of the Economic Contract Law in the Trial of Economic Contract Dispute Cases" and the "Answers to Questions Concerning the Specific Application of the Civil Procedure Law (for Trial Implementation) in the Trial of Economic Dispute Cases" are hereby issued to you for implementation in economic adjudication work. Any issues or opinions arising during implementation shall be promptly reported to this Court.

July 21, 1987

Supreme People's Court

Answers to Questions Concerning the Specific Application of the Economic Contract Law in the Trial of Economic Contract Dispute Cases

(July 21, 1987)

I. How to Determine the Qualification and Authority of an Agent When a Contract Signer Signs a Contract Without Holding a Formal Power of Attorney

Article 10 of the Economic Contract Law provides: "When concluding an economic contract through an agent, the agent must first obtain the entrustment certificate from the entrusting unit and sign the contract in the name of the entrusting unit within the authorized scope, in order to directly create rights and obligations for the entrusting unit." Article 65, paragraph 2 of the General Principles of the Civil Law provides: "A written power of attorney for agency by agreement shall clearly state the name or title of the agent, the matters of agency, the scope of authority, and the term, and shall be signed or sealed by the principal." For situations where some units authorize their own business personnel or entrust personnel from other units to sign contracts but do not issue a formal power of attorney, the determination of the contract signer's agency qualification and scope of authority requires specific analysis:

(1) If the contract signer signs the contract using the entrusting unit's special contract seal or a blank contract form bearing the official seal, it shall be deemed that the entrusting unit has granted the contract signer the authority of agency. The entrusting unit shall bear liability for the contract signed by the contract signer.

(2) If the contract signer signs the contract holding a letter of introduction issued by the entrusting unit, it shall be deemed that the entrusting unit has granted the authority of agency. If the letter of introduction does not clearly express the matters of agency or scope of authority, the entrusting unit shall bear liability for the contract, and the contract signer shall bear joint and several liability.

(3) If the contract signer signs the contract without holding any authorization certificate issued by the entrusting unit, and the entrusting unit has not affixed its seal, the contract shall not be established, and the liability shall be borne solely by the contract signer; if the entrusting unit has already commenced performance, it shall be deemed that the entrusting unit has ratified the contract signer's actions, and therefore shall bear liability for the contract; if further performance is required, the entrusting unit shall complete formalities such as affixing its seal.

II. How to Determine the Validity of Economic Contracts Signed Using Borrowed Business Letters of Introduction, Special Contract Seals, or Blank Contract Forms Bearing the Official Seal

A unit's business letter of introduction, special contract seal, and contract forms are important credentials for conducting external activities and shall not be lent or used for illegal profit-making. Economic contracts signed using borrowed business letters of introduction, special contract seals, or blank contract forms bearing the official seal of another unit shall be confirmed as invalid contracts. The lending unit and the borrower shall bear joint and several liability for the legal consequences of the invalid contract. Any "handling fees" or "management fees" collected by the lending unit shall be recovered as illegal income and turned over to the State Treasury.

If the borrower has a subordinate or contractual relationship with the lending unit, and the borrower signs the contract for legitimate business operations, the contract shall not be treated as an invalid contract. However, the lending unit shall bear joint and several compensatory liability with the borrower for the non-performance or incomplete performance of the contract.

If the contract signer steals and uses the unit's letter of introduction, special contract seal, or blank contract form bearing the official seal to sign an economic contract, the contract shall be confirmed as invalid, and all liability shall be borne solely by the thief; if the conduct constitutes a crime, the matter shall be promptly transferred to the public security or procuratorial authorities for handling.

III. How to Apply the State Council's Notice on Resolutely Curbing On-the-Spot Reselling Activities

The State Council issued the "Notice on Resolutely Curbing On-the-Spot Reselling Activities" (hereinafter referred to as the State Council Document No. 37 [1985]) on March 13, 1985. The State Administration for Industry and Commerce, the Ministry of Commerce, and the State Bureau of Materials, as well as the people's governments of various provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government, in accordance with State Council Document No. 37 [1985], stipulated the categories and scope of important means of production and durable consumer goods in short supply that are prohibited from being resold on the spot. Accordingly, for economic contracts signed after the issuance of State Council Document No. 37 [1985], any contract that violates the provisions of Document No. 37 shall be uniformly determined to be an invalid contract. For economic contracts signed before the issuance of State Council Document No. 37 [1985], they shall be handled appropriately based on different circumstances:

(1) If, at the time of signing, the contract content violated the relevant laws and policies of the State in effect at that time, the contract shall be determined to be invalid.

(2) If, at the time of signing, the contract content did not violate the laws and policies of the State in effect at that time, and the contract had been fully performed before the issuance of State Council Document No. 37 [1985], the contract may be determined to be valid.

(3) If, at the time of signing, the contract content did not violate the laws and policies of the State in effect at that time, but after the issuance of Document No. 37 [1985], the contract content violates the provisions of the document: if the contract has been partially performed, performance shall be terminated; if the contract has not been performed at all, the contract shall be dissolved according to law; disputes over property may be handled based on the actual circumstances.

IV. Whether Economic Contracts Signed Beyond the Business Scope or in Violation of Business Methods Are Valid

Industrial and commercial enterprises, individual industrial and commercial households, and other economic organizations shall engage in legitimate business operations within the business scope approved and registered by the administrative departments for industry and commerce or approved by the competent authorities. Contracts signed beyond the business scope or in violation of business methods shall be determined to be invalid contracts. For example: illegally dealing in important means of production and durable consumer goods in short supply; retail businesses engaging in wholesale operations; consignment agents engaging in distribution; imported goods permitted for sale only in specific areas being illegally transferred to other areas without approval, etc., all shall be treated as invalid contracts. If the entire contract involves matters beyond the business scope, the entire contract is invalid; if part of the contract involves matters beyond the business scope, that part shall be invalid.

V. How to Determine the Validity of Economic Contracts Signed by Industrial and Commercial Enterprises Without Actual Performance Capability

Parties entering into an economic contract shall have their own funds and the capability to perform the contract and bear liability commensurate with their business scope and scale. Currently, some industrial and commercial enterprises, although approved and registered by the administrative departments for industry and commerce and having obtained business licenses, knowingly lack the ability to perform the contract but still sign economic contracts with other units; such conduct is fraudulent in nature. Article 7, paragraph 1, item (2) of the Economic Contract Law provides that contracts entered into by means of fraud, duress, or the like are invalid. Therefore, economic contracts signed by such industrial and commercial enterprises without actual performance capability shall be determined to be invalid.

Some industrial and commercial enterprises may sign economic contracts that exceed their own funds or existing sources of goods, but if within the performance period stipulated in the contract, they can raise the necessary funds through legitimate channels, or through efforts can secure the required sources of goods, then the contract may be determined to be valid.

VI. How to Determine Illegal Acts Such as Signing Fictitious Economic Contracts, Scalping Economic Contracts, Engaging in Speculation Using Economic Contracts, and Profiteering from Subcontracting

Fictitious economic contracts are those where both parties maliciously collude to circumvent the law, achieve illegal purposes, and use deceptive means to sign an economic contract that is formally legal but that neither party actually intends to perform. Such fictitious economic contracts shall be determined to be invalid.

Scalping economic contracts occurs when one party to a contract resells to a third party at a markup an economic contract it has signed or obtained from another party, thereby seeking illegal profits. Such scalping of economic contracts shall be determined to be invalid. In practice, care must be taken to distinguish between illegal scalping of economic contracts and legal assignment of economic contracts. A legal assignment requires the consent of the other party to the contract, and the purpose is to enable the continued performance of the contract, not to seek illegal profits.

Engaging in speculation using economic contracts occurs when a party to a contract, having no funds of its own and no sources of goods, in violation of industrial and commercial administration regulations, uses the method of signing a contract, without the contract subject matter ever passing through its hands, to seek illegal profits. Such speculative economic contracts shall be determined to be invalid. In practice, care must be taken to distinguish speculation from a temporary lack of performance capability. If the supplier has no goods in stock but is an enterprise that produces such goods or a unit that has legitimate sources of supply for such goods, and is only temporarily unable to deliver due to some objective reason; or if the buyer temporarily lacks part of the funds but can resolve this through efforts, it shall not be considered speculation.

If the contractor under a construction project contract or the contractor under a processing contract, without the consent of the contract-issuing party or the ordering party, unauthorizedly subcontracts the contract to a third party and seeks illegal profits therefrom, this constitutes profiteering from subcontracting using an economic contract. Such subcontracting for profiteering shall be determined to be invalid. Care must be taken not to confuse lawful subcontracting with illegal subcontracting for profiteering.

Signing fictitious economic contracts, scalping economic contracts, engaging in speculation using economic contracts, and profiteering from subcontracting are all illegal acts. The illegal income derived therefrom shall be recovered, and depending on the circumstances, sanctions such as fines may be imposed according to law; if the circumstances are serious enough to constitute a crime, the matter shall be promptly transferred to the public security or procuratorial authorities for handling.

VII. How to Determine the Validity of Chain Purchase and Sale Contracts

Chain purchase and sale contracts refer to a series of purchase and sale contracts involving the same subject matter, i.e., after the buyer and seller sign a purchase and sale contract, the buyer, acting as a seller, signs another purchase and sale contract with a third party regarding the same subject matter, and so on, forming a chain relationship among the various purchase and sale contracts. The validity of each purchase and sale contract shall be determined based on the specific circumstances of that contract itself, i.e., by analyzing factors such as the subject matter of the contract, the legal person status, the scope of agency authority, the business scope, business methods, and the intent expressed at the time of contracting, to determine whether the contract is valid according to law.

VIII. Issues Concerning the Payment of Earnest Money (Deposit)

(1) Issues concerning the application of earnest money payment. Earnest money is a form of security for the performance of a contract. Whether to adopt this form of security is decided by the parties to the contract. The "Regulations on Purchase and Sale Contracts for Agricultural and Sideline Products," the "Regulations on Survey and Design Contracts for Construction Projects," and the "Regulations on Processing Contracts" provide for the payment of earnest money. Although the "Regulations on Purchase and Sale Contracts for Industrial and Mineral Products" do not provide for the payment of earnest money, according to Article 14 of the Economic Contract Law, which states that "one party may pay earnest money to the other party," the parties to an industrial and mineral products purchase and sale contract may agree to pay earnest money, and this shall be permitted.

(2) Issues concerning the amount of earnest money. If the regulations have specific provisions on the amount of earnest money, such provisions shall be followed; if the parties are allowed to agree on the amount, their agreement shall prevail. For example, Article 7, paragraph 2 of the "Regulations on Survey and Design Contracts for Construction Projects" provides: "The earnest money for survey tasks shall be 30% of the survey fee; the earnest money for design tasks shall be 20% of the estimated design fee." When signing a contract, the parties must comply with the specific amounts provided. Article 9 of the "Regulations on Processing Contracts" provides: "In accordance with relevant State regulations, the ordering party may pay earnest money to the contractor. The amount of earnest money shall be determined through negotiation between the parties." Therefore, if the amount of earnest money agreed upon by the parties to a processing contract does not violate relevant State regulations, it shall be permitted.

(3) Issues concerning whether the earnest money penalty rule applies to incomplete performance. Article 17, paragraph 6 and Article 18, paragraph 6 of the "Regulations on Purchase and Sale Contracts for Agricultural and Sideline Products" provide that if the supplier incompletely performs a pre-purchase contract, the supplier shall refund double the earnest money paid for the unperformed portion; if the buyer incompletely performs a pre-purchase contract, the buyer shall not be entitled to recover the earnest money paid for the unperformed portion. For other types of economic contracts where earnest money is permitted, the same principle may be applied in cases of incomplete performance.

(4) Issues concerning whether earnest money and liquidated damages can be applied concurrently. The natures of earnest money and liquidated damages are different. Earnest money is a form of security, whereas liquidated damages are a form of sanction and compensation for breach of contract. Therefore, if one party breaches the contract, the other party may demand both the payment of liquidated damages and the application of the earnest money penalty rule, provided that there are no contrary provisions in laws and regulations. Such concurrent application shall be protected, but the total result shall not exceed the total price of the contract subject matter.

IX. Issues Concerning the Application of Liquidated Damages

Article 35 of the Economic Contract Law provides: "If one party breaches an economic contract, it shall pay liquidated damages to the other party." The implementing regulations or detailed rules for various types of economic contracts issued by the State Council provide specific provisions on when and how liquidated damages shall be paid. When trying economic contract dispute cases, the people's courts shall handle the payment of liquidated damages in accordance with the provisions of the relevant implementing regulations or detailed rules for economic contracts:

(1) If the regulations or detailed rules specifically provide for the calculation standard of liquidated damages and do not allow the parties to agree otherwise, for example, Article 35, item (5), Article 36, items (3) and (4) of the "Regulations on Purchase and Sale Contracts for Industrial and Mineral Products," Article 18, items (3) and (5) of the "Regulations on Purchase and Sale Contracts for Agricultural and Sideline Products," Articles 15, 16, and 17 of the "Regulations on Loan Contracts," and Article 22, item (5) of the "Regulations on Processing Contracts," which provide that liquidated damages for delayed delivery, delayed taking delivery, or delayed payment shall be paid in accordance with the People's Bank of China's provisions on delayed payment, additional penalty interest, etc., or shall be paid as a certain percentage of the total price (or remuneration). If the parties violate these provisions and agree on a different amount of liquidated damages in the contract, such agreement shall be confirmed as invalid, and the provisions of the regulations shall still apply.

(2) If the regulations or detailed rules provide a range of proportional rates for liquidated damages and also allow the parties to agree on a specific proportion or amount within that legal range, for example, Article 35, item (1) and Article 36, item (1) of the "Regulations on Purchase and Sale Contracts for Industrial and Mineral Products," Article 17, items (1), (2), and (4) and Article 18, items (1) and (2) of the "Regulations on Purchase and Sale Contracts for Agricultural and Sideline Products," Article 13, item (2), sub-item (4) of the "Regulations on Construction and Installation Engineering Contracting Contracts," and Article 21, item (5) and Article 22, item (2) of the "Regulations on Processing Contracts," the liquidated damages agreed upon by the parties shall be recognized as valid if they fall within the legal proportional range; any portion exceeding the legal proportional range shall be confirmed as invalid; if the agreed amount is below the legal proportional range, the minimum provided by law shall apply.

(3) If the regulations or detailed rules provide a specific amount of liquidated damages but also allow the parties to agree otherwise in the contract without being restricted by such provisions, or stipulate that the parties' agreement shall prevail over the statutory provisions, for example, according to Article 25 of the "Detailed Rules for the Implementation of Storage and Warehousing Contracts" and Article 21, item (4) of the "Regulations on Processing Contracts," the parties to the contract have the right to freely negotiate the amount of liquidated damages outside the statutory scope. Such agreements by the parties shall be recognized as valid.

(4) If the regulations or detailed rules do not provide specific provisions on liquidated damages and leave the matter entirely to the parties' agreement, for example, Article 13, item (1), sub-item (2) and item (2), sub-item (4) of the "Regulations on Construction and Installation Engineering Contracting Contracts" provide that if the time for completion and delivery of the project by the contractor fails to meet the requirements, or if the contract-issuing party fails to accept the project beyond the date specified in the contract, liquidated damages for delay shall be paid in accordance with the provisions on liability for breach of contract in the contract. Such agreements by the parties in the contract shall be recognized as valid.

However, in the circumstances described in (3) and (4) above, to prevent the parties from abusing the right to agree freely, the amount of liquidated damages shall generally not exceed the total price of the unperformed portion of the contract; any amount exceeding that may not be protected by the court.

X. How to Handle the Situation Where a Township (Town) or Village Enterprise Is Insolvent

If a township (town) or village-run enterprise becomes insolvent or goes bankrupt due to losses or other reasons, the question of who shall bear liability for the contractual debts left behind shall be determined based on the following distinction: if the enterprise has independent legal person status, the enterprise itself shall be liable; if it does not have independent legal person status, its competent authority shall bear joint and several liability for repayment.

Supreme People's Court

Answers to Questions Concerning the Specific Application of the Civil Procedure Law (for Trial Implementation) in the Trial of Economic Dispute Cases

(July 21, 1987)

I. Issues Concerning Territorial Jurisdiction in Chain Purchase and Sale Contract Dispute Cases

Chain purchase and sale contracts often span several regions. A dispute arising from one contract may affect other contracts. For chain purchase and sale contract dispute cases, generally, the courts with jurisdiction shall handle them separately. When necessary, parties that have a direct interest in the preceding or subsequent contracts may be added as third parties to the case and notified to participate in the proceedings. If such chain purchase and sale contracts have already been separately tried by several courts, the courts shall proactively contact and cooperate with each other and may consult on jurisdiction issues. If, after consultation, it is deemed more appropriate to handle the chain purchase and sale contract dispute in a single proceeding, a single court may assume unified jurisdiction. If the chain purchase and sale contract involves a crime, the matter shall be promptly transferred to the public security or procuratorial authorities for handling in accordance with regulations.

II. Issues Concerning the Resolution of Jurisdictional Disputes

Article 33, paragraph 2 of the Civil Procedure Law (for Trial Implementation) provides: "If a dispute over jurisdiction arises, it shall be resolved through consultation between the disputing parties; if consultation fails to resolve the matter, the matter shall be submitted to the common superior people's court for designation of jurisdiction." Accordingly, if two basic courts within the same prefecture or municipality have a jurisdictional dispute that cannot be resolved through consultation, the matter shall be designated by the intermediate people's court of that prefecture or municipality. If two courts within the same province, autonomous region, or municipality directly under the Central Government have a jurisdictional dispute that cannot be resolved through consultation, the matter shall be designated by the high people's court of that province, autonomous region, or municipality. If two courts from different provinces, autonomous regions, or municipalities directly under the Central Government have a jurisdictional dispute that cannot be resolved through consultation, the matter shall be submitted to the respective high people's courts of the two provinces, autonomous regions, or municipalities for resolution through consultation; if the two high people's courts cannot resolve the matter after consultation, each shall submit its opinion to the Supreme People's Court for designation of jurisdiction.

If a party to a case objects to jurisdiction, the objection shall be raised to the court hearing the case. Before conducting a substantive trial of the case, the court hearing the case shall first consider the party's objection to jurisdiction and make a written ruling in accordance with law on whether the court has jurisdiction over the case. The ruling shall be served on both parties. If a party is dissatisfied with the ruling, it has the right to appeal to the next higher people's court. After the court of second instance determines the jurisdiction of the case, the parties shall participate in the proceedings in accordance with the court's notice.

III. Issues Concerning Who Shall Appear as the Defendant After the Closure of Township (Town) or Village Enterprises or Street Enterprises That Do Not Have Legal Person Status

If township (town) or village enterprises or street enterprises that do not have legal person status are closed due to poor management or changes in the management system, their competent authority or sponsoring unit shall appear as the defendant in litigation involving them.

4. Regarding the Issue of Who Shall Be the Party in Litigation for a Joint Operation Organization or Partnership Organization That Does Not Meet the Requirements for Legal Person Status

Economic combinations that emerged during the economic system reform and do not meet the requirements for legal person status include, in some cases, joint operations between enterprises or between enterprises and institutions, and in other cases, partnerships of two or more individuals. However, these organizations are formed in accordance with joint operation or partnership agreements, which stipulate matters such as the amount of capital contribution by each party, distribution of profits, and assumption of debts. When such a joint operation organization or partnership organization that does not have legal person status becomes involved in an economic dispute and files a lawsuit with the court, if it has a business name, the name approved according to law shall be used as the litigation subject, and the head of the organization shall act as the litigation representative; if it does not have a business name, the parties forming the joint operation organization or the partners of the partnership organization shall participate in the litigation as co-litigants. If there are many parties to the joint operation or partners, they may elect a representative to conduct the litigation, and the litigation acts of such representative shall be binding on all parties to the joint operation or partners.

5. Regarding the Litigation Status of the Lender and Borrower in Cases of Illegal Lending of Business Introduction Letters, Special Contract Seals, or Blank Contracts

Business introduction letters, special contract seals, or stamped blank contracts of enterprises and institutions are exclusively for the normal business use of the unit and shall not be lent to others. If a unit illegally lends its business introduction letter, special contract seal, or stamped blank contract to another person for the purpose of entering into an economic contract, regardless of the lender's intent, the lender has become a party to the economic contract and, together with the borrower, shall participate in the litigation concerning that economic contract as co-litigants. If the lender and the borrower are the defendants, they shall be listed as co-defendants; if the borrower files a lawsuit but the lender does not, the people's court shall, in accordance with Article 91 of the Civil Procedure Law (for Trial Implementation), notify the lender to participate in the litigation.

6. Regarding the Litigation Status of the Guarantor of an Economic Contract

Article 89, paragraph 1, of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC provides: "A guarantor guarantees to the creditor that the debtor will perform the obligation. If the debtor fails to perform the obligation, the guarantor shall perform the obligation or assume joint and several liability in accordance with the agreement." Article 15 of the Economic Contract Law of the PRC also provides: "The guaranteeing unit is a person concerned who guarantees that one party to the contract will perform the contract. When the guaranteed party fails to perform the contract, the guaranteeing unit shall be jointly and severally liable for the loss." Therefore, in litigation, the guarantor and the guaranteed party shall be listed as co-defendants. After the guarantor has assumed the liability for compensation on behalf of the guaranteed party, it has the right to recover the amount from the guaranteed party. If the guaranteed party has terminated or ceased to exist, the guarantor may be named as the defendant.

7. Regarding the Litigation Rights and Obligations of a Third Party Without Independent Claim

When a third party without independent claim applies to participate in the litigation, or when the people's court considers it necessary for such a third party to participate in the litigation, the court shall notify the third party to participate by a notice. After the third party without independent claim participates in the litigation, it has the right to be informed of the facts and reasons of the plaintiff's complaint and the defendant's defense, and to submit a written statement of opinion to the people's court, setting forth its own views on the dispute. At the trial, the people's court shall summon the third party to appear in court by a subpoena. During the court hearing, the third party without independent claim may present opinions, provide evidence, and participate in the court debate. If, after two lawful summonses, the third party without independent claim refuses to appear in court without justifiable reason, the people's court may render a default judgment. If a legally effective judgment, ruling, or mediation agreement of the people's court determines that the third party without independent claim shall assume certain obligations, the third party must perform those obligations; if it refuses to perform without justifiable reason, the people's court may enforce compulsory execution.

8. Regarding the Issue of How to Emphasize Mediation in the Trial of Economic Dispute Cases

When trying economic dispute cases, the people's court shall also emphasize mediation. However, mediation is not a mandatory procedure. For economic administrative cases, cases confirming the invalidity of contracts, and cases involving illegal or criminal activities, mediation shall not be conducted. When handling a case, whether to mediate or adjudicate shall be decided based on the actual circumstances: mediation should be used when possible, and adjudication should be used when appropriate. Courts shall neither unilaterally pursue the rate of mediation settlement, resulting in prolonged mediation without resolution, nor fail to mediate when possible and simply render a judgment to dispose of the case.

Mediation shall be conducted on the basis of ascertaining the facts and distinguishing right from wrong. Courts shall not mediate without investigating, or investigate only after mediation. Whether the case is concluded by mediation or by judgment, the determination of the rights, obligations, rights and wrongs, and responsibilities of the parties shall be consistent. Courts shall not "gloss over differences" without principle, or avoid the fault liability for breach of contract simply because the case is concluded by mediation.

Mediation must adhere to the principles of voluntariness and legality. Through legal education, guidance, and persuasion, the court shall encourage the parties to voluntarily and willingly reach a mediation agreement, and shall not force mediation or force mediation in disguised form. The outcome of a case concluded by mediation may differ from that concluded by judgment, but it shall not violate the law or policies.
